title: Sentence Stress

revision.summary: Learn to stress the content words in a sentence (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, negatives) and reduce the small words, so your English sounds natural and clear.
examples: I WANT to BUY a new PHONE.

body_content:
Sentence Stress

English is a stress-timed language: some words are long and clear, others are short and quiet. Stressed words carry the meaning. If you stress every word equally, listeners find it hard to follow you.

1. Content words and function words

  • Content words are stressed: nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, negatives, question words.
  • Function words are usually weak: articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns.

Example: I WANT to BUY a new PHONE. Read it and clap on the capital words only.

2. Rhythm

The time between stressed words stays about the same. So "Cats eat fish" and "The cats are eating the fish" take almost the same time. In the second sentence the small words are squeezed together.

3. Changing the meaning

Stress can show what is important or new. Listen: I didn't take your book. (someone else did) / I didn't TAKE your book. (I borrowed it) / I didn't take YOUR book. (I took another one).

4. Word stress in noun and verb pairs

Some two-syllable words change stress: a REcord (noun) and to reCORD (verb); a PREsent and to preSENT.

5. Where accents differ

Sentence stress works the same way in both accents. Some individual words are stressed differently:

UKadVERtisement = /ədˈvɜːtɪsmənt/
garage = /ˈɡærɑːʒ/ or /ˈɡærɪdʒ/
laboratory = /ləˈbɒrətri/
USadvertISEment = /ˌædvərˈtaɪzmənt/
garage = /ɡəˈrɑːʒ/
laboratory = /ˈlæbrətɔːri/
Practice tip: take any sentence, underline the content words, and say only those words. Then add the small words quickly between them.

title: Linking Words in Speech

revision.summary: Learn how English speakers link the end of one word to the start of the next (consonant-vowel, vowel-vowel, same consonant) so you can say and understand fast speech.

body_content:
Linking Words in Speech

In natural speech there are no gaps between words. The end of one word joins the start of the next. Learning the main links helps you speak smoothly and understand fast speakers.

1. Consonant + vowel

When a word ends in a consonant sound and the next word starts with a vowel, the consonant moves across: turn off sounds like "tur-noff", check in sounds like "che-kin", pick it up sounds like "pi-ki-tup".

2. Vowel + vowel

A small sound joins two vowels. After /iː/, /aɪ/, /eɪ/ it is /j/: I am = "I-y-am", she asked = "she-y-asked". After /uː/, /əʊ/ it is /w/: go on = "go-w-on", do it = "do-w-it".

3. Same consonant twice

When the same consonant sound ends one word and starts the next, say it once but a little longer: black cat, big game, some more.

4. Where accents differ

Linking is common in both accents. The difference is the "r":

UKfar away = "fah-r-away" (r appears only before a vowel)
car park = "cah park" (no r)
here it is = "here-r-it is" (linking r)
USfar away = "far away" (r is always pronounced)
car park = "car park" (r pronounced)
here it is = "here it is" (r already there)
Practice tip: write a sentence, draw a small line under each link, and say it without stops.

title: Intonation in Questions

revision.summary: Learn the rising and falling intonation of yes/no questions, wh- questions, question tags and lists, and how it shows meaning and attitude.
examples: You're coming, aren't you? (rising = asking, falling = checking)

body_content:
Intonation in Questions

Intonation is the music of your voice: it goes up and down. It shows if you are asking, checking, or being polite or bored. Listen for the pitch on the last stressed word.

1. Yes/no questions

The voice usually rises at the end: Are you ready? Do you like it? The rise shows you are waiting for an answer.

2. Wh- questions

The voice usually falls at the end: Where do you live? What time is it? A rising voice on a wh- question sounds more friendly or is used to ask for repetition: "You live WHERE?"

3. Question tags

With a rising tag you really ask: You're coming, aren't you? (I do not know.) With a falling tag you expect agreement: Nice day, isn't it?

4. Lists

In a list the voice rises on each item and falls on the last: "We need eggs (↗), milk (↗), bread (↗) and butter (↘)."

5. Where accents differ

Both accents use the patterns above. Some differences in everyday speech:

UKRight? and Yeah? at the end for checking
Polite questions often have a bigger rise
Many statements can end with a small rise in regions such as Northern Ireland
USRight? and OK? at the end for checking
Some speakers use a rising tone on statements ("uptalk")
Wh- questions usually fall
Practice tip: ask the same question two ways, rising and falling, and notice how the meaning changes.

title: Listening: Interviews

revision.summary: Practise listening to job and news interviews, catching questions, main answers and examples, with UK and US vocabulary differences.
examples: Tell me about your last job.
I've worked as a nurse for five years.

body_content:
Listening: Interviews

Interviews follow a pattern: a question, a main answer and often an example. If you follow this pattern, you can understand long answers.

1. Listening strategy

  • First listen for the question (what does the speaker want to know?).
  • Then find the main answer (it is usually in the first sentence).
  • Finally catch an example (signalled by for example, for instance, when I).

2. Script 1: a job interview

A: Tell me about your last job.
B: I've worked as a nurse for five years at a city hospital. For example, I trained new staff and organised the night shifts.
A: Why do you want to change?
B: I'd like more responsibility and to learn new skills.

Main answers: nurse, five years and more responsibility. Example: trained new staff.

3. Script 2: a radio interview

A: You've just opened a bakery. How is business?
B: Better than expected. We were busy from the first day, mainly because people heard about us online.
A: What is your plan for next year?
B: We hope to open a second shop.

Key details: better than expected, online, second shop.

4. Signal phrases

  • Mainly, mostly = the biggest reason.
  • However, but = a contrast is coming.
  • In the future, next year = a plan.

5. Where UK and US differ

UKCV = document about your career
notice period for leaving a job
holiday = time off
USresume = document about your career
two weeks' notice for leaving a job
vacation = time off
Practice tip: listen to a short interview and write the question, the main answer and one example.

title: Listening: Short Talks

revision.summary: Practise following short talks by catching the topic, the order of ideas (first, then, finally) and the main message, with UK and US differences.
examples: Today I'm going to talk about...

body_content:
Listening: Short Talks

A short talk has a beginning, a middle and an end. The speaker usually tells you the topic first and uses signal words to show the order of ideas.

1. Script 1: a talk about sleep

Today I'm going to talk about sleep. First, most adults need seven to eight hours a night. Second, screens before bed make it harder to fall asleep. Finally, a regular routine really helps. So, the main point is simple: go to bed at the same time every night.

Topic: sleep. Ideas: 7-8 hours, screens, routine. Main message: same time every night.

2. Script 2: a talk about a town

I'd like to tell you about my home town. It is small, but it has a beautiful old market. Many visitors come in summer. However, in winter it is very quiet, and that is why I love it.

Contrast word: however. The speaker's feeling: loves the quiet winter.

3. Signal words for order and contrast

  • First, second, then, next, finally = order.
  • However, but, although = contrast.
  • So, in short, the main point is = the conclusion.

4. Where UK and US differ

UKat the weekend
autumn
fortnight = two weeks
maths
USon the weekend
fall
two weeks
math
Practice tip: after listening to a talk, say the topic and three main ideas in your own words.

title: Listening: Phone Calls

revision.summary: Practise listening to phone calls, catching the reason for the call, spelled names, numbers and next steps, with UK and US phone language.
examples: Could I speak to Ms Brown, please?
I'll call you back. (UK also: ring)

body_content:
Listening: Phone Calls

On the phone you cannot see faces, so you must listen carefully. Follow four steps: who is calling, why, the key details (names, numbers, times) and the next step.

1. Script 1: making an appointment

A: Good morning, Riverside Dental.
B: Hello, I'd like to make an appointment for a check-up.
A: Certainly. Is Thursday at ten possible?
B: Could we do Friday? I'm working on Thursday.
A: Friday at eleven thirty is free.
B: Perfect. It's Carla Nunez. That's N-U-N-E-Z.

Why: check-up. Details: Friday, 11:30, name Nunez.

2. Script 2: leaving a message

A: Could I speak to Mr Hall, please?
B: I'm afraid he's in a meeting. Can I take a message?
A: Yes, please tell him Ann called about the report. My number is 0161 555 0123.
B: I'll pass that on.

Next step: Mr Hall will get the message.

3. Useful phrases

  • Speaking. = I am the person you want.
  • Hold on. / Hold the line. = wait.
  • Could you spell that, please? = ask for the spelling.
  • I'm afraid... = polite bad news.

4. Where UK and US differ

UKMr Hall (no full stop)
ring / call someone
Who's calling?
mobile
USMr. Hall (with a full stop)
call someone
Who's this?
cell phone
Practice tip: ask a friend to spell a name to you over the phone and write it down before you check.

title: Mixed Conditionals
body_content:
Practice Mixed Conditionals.

Say it: 'd have and 'd in mixed conditionals

In mixed conditionals the contracted forms blur: I'd have /aɪd əv/ and I'd /aɪd/ sound almost the same. Have is reduced to /əv/. Stress the two key verbs: If I'd STUDied law, I'd be a LAWyer now.

Say it: "If I'd taken that job, I'd be living abroad now."

audio_urls.title: Say it: 'd have and 'd in mixed conditionals

title: Inversion
body_content:
Practice Inversion.

Say it: stress in negative inversion

After a fronted negative adverbial the auxiliary comes before the subject, and the fronted phrase takes the stress: NEVer have I SEEN such a mess. Pause briefly after the fronted phrase, then keep the rest smooth: Not ONly did she WIN | but she broke the RECord.

Say it: "Under no circumstances should you open this door."

audio_urls.title: Say it: stress in negative inversion

title: Modal Perfect
body_content:
Practice Modal Perfect.

Say it: modal perfect: have is weak

In modal perfects have is reduced to /əv/ and often sounds like of: should have /ʃʊd əv/, might have /maɪt əv/. Write have, never of. Stress the modal for judgement and the participle for content: You SHOULD have TOLD me.

Where accents differ

UKneedn't have gone
USdidn't need to go (more common)
Say it: "She must have left. He can't have known. You should have told me."

audio_urls.title: Say it: modal perfect: have is weak

title: Causative
body_content:
Practice Causative.

Say it: have / get something done

Stress the thing done and the participle: I had my HAIR CUT. I'm getting the CAR serviced. Have is usually weak: I'll have it fixed /aɪl həv ɪt fɪkst/.

Where accents differ

UKI'm having the boiler serviced.
I had my flat repainted.
USI'm getting the furnace serviced.
I got my apartment painted.
Say it: "She had her passport renewed. We're getting the roof repaired."

audio_urls.title: Say it: have / get something done

title: Concession
body_content:
Practice Concession.

Listen for: concession in speech

Though at the end of a sentence is a common spoken concession, often with a fall-rise: It was expensive. Worth it, though. However is usually followed by a pause. After although, listen for the stressed contrast: Although it was RAINing, we went OUT.

Where accents differ

UKAll the same, even so
Mind you (informal): Mind you, it was cheap.
USStill, even so
Then again: Then again, it was cheap.
Listen for: "Nice hotel. Noisy, though. Even so, we'd go back."

title: Habit in the Present and the Past

revision.summary: Practice Habit in the Present and the Past.

body_content:
Practice Habit in the Present and the Past.

Listen for: used to and would for habits

Used to is /ˈjuːst tə/ (the d disappears): We used to LIVE there. Would for past habits is contracted: We'd go every SUMmer. Listen for time words such as every, always and when I was young.

Where accents differ

UKI used not to (formal)
I usedn't to (rare)
USI didn't use to
I never used to
Listen for: "We used to go every summer. We'd swim before breakfast."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: used to and would for habits

revision.summary: Practice Present Perfect Simple and Continuous.

title: Past Simple, Past Continuous, Past Perfect

revision.summary: Practice Past Simple, Past Continuous, Past Perfect.

body_content:
Practice Past Simple, Past Continuous, Past Perfect.

Say it: -ed endings and 'd had

The past simple -ed has three sounds: /t/ after voiceless sounds (worked), /d/ after voiced sounds (played /pleɪd/), /ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/ (wanted). In the past perfect, had is weak or contracted: She'd already left /ʃiːd ɔːlˈredi left/.

Where accents differ

UKworked /wɜːkt/
wanted /ˈwɒntɪd/
USworked /wɜːrkt/
wanted /ˈwɑːntɪd/
Say it: "I worked all day. I'd already finished when she arrived."

title: Question tags
body_content:
Practice Question tags.

Say it: question tags: agree or ask

A falling tag seeks agreement: Nice day, isn't it ↘. A rising tag is a real question: You're coming, aren't you ↗? Keep the tag short and light: /ˈɪznt ɪt/.

Where accents differ

UKI'm late, aren't I?
Let's go, shall we?
USI'm late, aren't I?
Let's go, okay?
Say it: "It's cold, isn't it? You haven't seen it, have you?"

audio_urls.title: Say it: question tags: agree or ask

title: Future forms
body_content:
Practice Future forms.

Say it: 'll, going to and present continuous

Going to often sounds like gonna /ˈɡʌnə/ in speech. I'll /aɪl/ is quick and light: I'll call you. The present continuous for plans stresses the time: I'm meeting her on FRIday. Write going to in formal writing.

Say it: "I'll call you later. I'm going to study. We're meeting on Friday."

audio_urls.title: Say it: 'll, going to and present continuous

title: Future Perfect
body_content:
Practice Future Perfect.

Say it: 'll have in the future perfect

Will have shrinks to 'll have /əl əv/: By June I'll have finished /baɪ dʒuːn aɪl əv ˈfɪnɪʃt/. Stress the time expression and the participle: By FRIday, they'll have FINished.

Say it: "By this time next year, she'll have graduated."

audio_urls.title: Say it: 'll have in the future perfect

revision.summary: Practice Zero, first, second, third conditionals.

title: Wish and if only
body_content:
Practice Wish and if only.

Say it: I wish I were / was

Both I wish I were and I wish I was are used; were is more formal. Reduce I wish I and stress the wished-for idea. If only is stressed strongly: If ONly I had more TIME.

Say it: "I wish I were taller. If only I had listened."

audio_urls.title: Say it: I wish I were / was

title: Compounds of some, any, no, every

revision.summary: Practice Compounds of some, any, no, every.

title: Relative clauses
body_content:
Practice Relative clauses.

Listen for: pauses in relative clauses

Non-defining clauses are set off by pauses (commas in writing): My brother, | who lives in Leeds, | is a nurse. Defining clauses have no pauses: The man who lives next door is a nurse. The pauses change the meaning: the first suggests I have only one brother.

Listen for: "My sister, who lives in Rome, is a doctor. The sister who lives in Rome is a doctor."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: pauses in relative clauses

title: Conjunctions: although, despite, in spite of, otherwise, unless

revision.summary: Practice Conjunctions: although, despite, in spite of, otherwise, unless.

body_content:
Practice Conjunctions: although, despite, in spite of, otherwise, unless.

Listen for: although, despite, unless

Although is stressed on the second syllable: alTHOUGH it was late. Despite and in spite of are followed by a noun or -ing: despite the RAIN. Unless /ənˈles/ is weak at the start.

Where accents differ

UKalthough /ɔːlˈðəʊ/
whilst (formal)
USalthough /ɔːlˈðoʊ/
while
Listen for: "Although it was late, we stayed. Unless it rains, we'll go."

revision.summary: Practice Adverbs of manner and modifiers.

title: Affixes
body_content:
Practice Affixes.

Say it: stress with suffixes

Some suffixes move stress: PHOtograph → phoTOGrapher → photoGRAPHic. -tion and -ic put stress on the syllable before: eduCAtion, ecoNOMic. Prefixes like un-, re-, dis- usually keep the stress: HAPpy → unHAPpy.

Where accents differ

UKsecretary /ˈsekrətri/
missile /ˈmɪsaɪl/
USsecretary /ˈsekrəteri/
missile /ˈmɪsl/
Say it: "photograph, photographer, photographic; economy, economic."

title: Crime and punishment — B2 legal process

revision.summary: Practice Crime and punishment — B2 legal process.

title: Relationships
body_content:
Practice Relationships.

Listen for: closeness in tone

The same words can sound close or distant. We're just friends. with a fall sounds final; with a fall-rise it leaves doubt. Listen for stress on just and really: We're JUST friends.

Where accents differ

UKget on with someone
fancy someone
USget along with someone
have a crush on someone
Listen for: "We get on really well. We're just friends."

title: Festivals and celebrations
body_content:
Practice Festivals and celebrations.

Listen for: festival vocabulary and stress

Stress in festival words: CELebrate, celeBRAtion, FEStival, TRAdition, fireworks /ˈfaɪəwɜːks/. Listen for stress on the event name and the day in invitations: See you at the PARty on SAturday.

Where accents differ

UKBonfire Night, Boxing Day
USFourth of July, Thanksgiving
Listen for: "The festival starts on Friday. Fireworks begin at nine."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: festival vocabulary and stress

title: Idiomatic expressions
body_content:
Practice Idiomatic expressions.

Listen for: idioms in connected speech

Idioms are often said as one chunk, with the stress on the last content word: it's a piece of CAKE, let's call it a DAY. Expect reductions: a piece of /ə ˈpiːs əv/. Listen for the chunk, not the individual words.

Where accents differ

UKa storm in a teacup
bob's your uncle
USa tempest in a teapot
hit a home run
Listen for: "It's a piece of cake. Let's call it a day."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: idioms in connected speech

title: Geography and climate
body_content:
Practice Geography and climate.

Say it: place names and climate words

English place names often break spelling rules: Thames /temz/, Worcester /ˈwʊstə/, Arctic /ˈɑːktɪk/ (say the first c). Learn stress for climate words: CLImate, TROpical, TEMperature.

Where accents differ

UKtropical /ˈtrɒpɪkl/
temperature /ˈtemprətʃə/
UStropical /ˈtrɑːpɪkl/
temperature /ˈtemprətʃər/
Say it: "The Thames is cold. The Arctic climate is harsh."

audio_urls.title: Say it: place names and climate words

title: Expressing regret
body_content:
Practice Expressing regret.

Say it: regret in your voice

Regret uses a falling tone and stress on the key word: I WISH I'd said something. If only I'd LISTened. Have is weak: I should have called /aɪ ʃʊd əv kɔːld/. A slower pace and lower pitch sound sincere.

Say it: "I should have called. I wish I'd listened."

audio_urls.title: Say it: regret in your voice

title: Stating contrast — conversational
body_content:
Practice Stating contrast — conversational.

Listen for: contrast in conversation

Spoken contrast: Yeah, but... starts a disagreement, Still,... accepts a point then reverses it. Listen for a fall-rise on the first idea and a fall on the contrast: It's ↘↗cheap, but it's ↘slow.

Where accents differ

UKMind you, it's cheap.
USThen again, it's cheap.
Listen for: "It's cheap, but it's slow. Still, it works."

title: Clarifying
body_content:
Practice Clarifying.

Say it: checking and clarifying

To check you understood, use a rising tone: So you mean the FIRST one? To ask for repetition politely: Sorry, could you say that again? To correct, stress the changed word: Not Tuesday, THURSday.

Where accents differ

UKSorry? / Pardon?
USExcuse me? / Come again? (informal)
Say it: "Sorry, do you mean the first one? Not Tuesday, Thursday."

title: Connected Speech

revision.summary: Learn how sounds change, disappear or join in fast speech (assimilation, elision, weak forms) so you can speak fluently and understand native speakers.

body_content:
Connected Speech

In careful speech every word is separate. In real speech, sounds change to make speaking easier. Learning these patterns helps you understand fast speakers and sound more natural.

1. Elision: sounds disappear

A /t/ or /d/ between two consonants often disappears: next day = "nex day", old man = "ol man", last night = "las night". Also inside words: friendship = "frenship".

2. Assimilation: sounds change

A sound becomes more like the next one: handbag = "hambag", ten pounds = "tem pounds", good boy = "goob boy", this shop = "thish shop".

3. Weak forms and contractions

Grammar words shrink: and = /ən/, of = /əv/, have = /əv/ in should have = "should've". Informal spelling shows this: gonna, wanna, gotta. Use them to understand, and be careful in formal writing.

4. Where accents differ

Both accents connect speech, but the patterns are not the same:

UKa lot of = "a lot ov" (t is clear)
Have you got...? is common
Shall we?
USa lot of = "a lodda" (t sounds like d)
Do you have...? is common
Should we?
Practice tip: record a short sentence at natural speed and compare it with the written words. Note which sounds disappear.

title: Contrastive Stress

revision.summary: Learn to move the main stress to a word to correct, contrast or emphasise information, and to hear the speaker's meaning from where the stress falls.
examples: I didn't say HE stole it.

body_content:
Contrastive Stress

Normally the main stress falls on the last content word: I bought a new CAR. With contrastive stress you move it to show a contrast, a correction or a surprise.

1. Correcting information

A: Is the meeting on Monday? B: No, it's on TUESday. The stressed word is the new information.

2. Showing a contrast

I like TEA, but she likes COFFEE. Both stressed words are the pair being compared.

3. One sentence, different meanings

Say "I didn't say he stole it" seven times, stressing a different word each time. Each version means something different: I didn't say it (someone else did); I didn't say it (I wrote it); he stole (he borrowed).

4. Numbers and letters

Stress the part that is different: fifTEEN or FIFty; B as in Bravo, not P. This is very useful on the phone.

5. Where accents differ

Contrastive stress works the same in both accents. Some words that you contrast may differ:

UKfortnight (two weeks) not week
flat, not house
autumn, not summer
UStwo weeks, not one week
apartment, not house
fall, not summer
Practice tip: correct a false statement out loud. "It's in Paris." "No, it's in ROME."

title: UK and US: /r/ and /t/

revision.summary: Compare how British and American English say /r/ after vowels and /t/ between vowels (flapping, glottal stops), so you can recognise both and choose one to use.

body_content:
UK and US: /r/ and /t/

The two biggest differences between standard British and American pronunciation are the letter r and the letter t. Knowing the rules makes both accents easy to understand.

1. The letter r

American English is rhotic: r is always pronounced. Standard British English is non-rhotic: r is pronounced only before a vowel.

UKcar = /kɑː/
park = /pɑːk/
teacher = /ˈtiːtʃə/
car alarm = /kɑːr əˈlɑːm/ (linking r)
UScar = /kɑːr/
park = /pɑːrk/
teacher = /ˈtiːtʃər/
car alarm = /kɑːr əˈlɑːrm/

2. The letter t between vowels

In American English /t/ between two vowels (when the second is unstressed) becomes a quick flap like a soft /d/: water, better, city. So latter and ladder sound almost the same.

UKwater = /ˈwɔːtə/ (clear t)
better = /ˈbetə/
bottle = often /ˈbɒʔl/ (glottal stop in informal speech)
USwater = /ˈwɔːɾər/ (flap)
better = /ˈbeɾər/
bottle = /ˈbɑːɾl/

3. Which to learn?

Choose one accent as your model and stay consistent. Practise recognising the other by listening to films, podcasts and news from both countries.

Practice tip: say "better butter" in both ways: with a clear t (UK) and a flap (US).

title: Listening: Podcasts

revision.summary: Practise listening to conversational podcasts, following opinions, informal language and jumps in topic, with UK and US vocabulary differences.
examples: To be honest, I wasn't convinced.
Anyway, going back to what I said...

body_content:
Listening: Podcasts

Podcasts are natural and informal. Speakers interrupt, change topic and use fillers. To follow them, listen for the topic, each speaker's opinion and the discourse markers that show the structure.

1. Script 1: two hosts

A: So, what did you think of the new city bike scheme?
B: To be honest, I wasn't convinced at first. I mean, the bikes are heavy. But actually, after a week I was hooked.
A: Really? Anyway, the price is what surprised me. A pound for thirty minutes!
B: Right, which is cheaper than the bus.

Opinions: B changes from not convinced to hooked. A is surprised by the price.

2. Discourse markers

  • To be honest, I mean, actually = the speaker gives an opinion or correction.
  • Anyway = change topic or return to the topic.
  • Right, exactly, I know = agreement.
  • By the way = a side comment.

3. Script 2: a story

So last week I was driving to work, and, you won't believe this, a lorry stopped in front of me and the driver got out to buy a sandwich! I mean, in the middle of the road!

Notice So (start of a story) and you won't believe this (something surprising). The listener does not need to catch every word.

4. Where UK and US differ

UKlorry, flat, mate
I reckon
quite good = fairly good
UStruck, apartment, buddy
I guess
pretty good = fairly good
Practice tip: play a podcast for two minutes, then write the topic, one opinion and the discourse markers you noticed.

title: Listening: Lectures and Note-taking

revision.summary: Practise listening to short lectures and taking notes: catching the main idea, signposts, key terms and examples, and writing them down with abbreviations.
examples: e.g. = for example; i.e. = that is

body_content:
Listening: Lectures and Note-taking

Lecturers give a lot of information in a short time. You cannot write every word. You need to listen for structure and write only key words.

1. Listen for signposts

  • Today I'll talk about... = topic.
  • There are three main causes = number of points.
  • First, second, finally = order.
  • This means that, in other words = an explanation.
  • For example = an example.
  • To sum up = the conclusion.

2. Script: a short lecture

Today I'll talk about urban heat islands. Cities are often hotter than the countryside, and there are two main causes. First, dark surfaces like roads absorb heat. Second, there are fewer trees, which means less shade and less cooling. For example, some cities are up to five degrees warmer at night. To sum up, planting trees and using lighter materials can help.

3. Model notes

Topic: urban heat islands (cities hotter)
Causes: 1) dark surfaces absorb heat 2) fewer trees = less shade
Ex: up to 5° warmer at night
Solution: trees + light materials

4. Abbreviations and symbols

e.g. = for example; i.e. = that is; = = means; → = leads to; w/ = with; & = and. Use numbers instead of words and keep only nouns, verbs and numbers.

5. Where UK and US differ

UKlecturer, module, revise for an exam
Uni / university
maths
USprofessor, course, review for a test
college / school (university)
math
Practice tip: after each lecture, rewrite your notes in a clear format and cover them to see what you remember.

title: Listening: Accents

revision.summary: Practise understanding different accents (British, American, Australian, Indian and others) by listening for stress and key words, with strategies for when speech is unfamiliar.
examples: Could you say that again, please?

body_content:
Listening: Accents

English is spoken by more people as a second language than as a first language. You will hear many accents at work, on trips and online. Every accent is different, but the grammar and stressed words are similar.

1. Strategies

  • Focus on stressed words.
  • Use context: topic, situation, gestures.
  • Expect the same word to sound different: a different vowel, a different r, a different t.
  • Ask politely: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you say it again, please?

2. Some typical patterns

  • Scottish and Irish English: r is often rolled or clear; vowels are often shorter.
  • Australian English: "day" sounds nearer to "die"; the rising tone is common on statements.
  • Indian English: syllables have similar length, and t and d are often made with the tongue touching the teeth.
  • General American: r is clear, t between vowels is a flap.

3. Script: a conversation between two accents

A (Australian): G'day! Are you free at three?
B (American): Three? Sorry, I didn't catch that. Did you say three or thirty?
A: Three. No worries, I'll say it again: at three o'clock.
B: Got it. See you then.

Note: B checks the number and A repeats it clearly. This is a good real-life strategy.

4. Where UK and US differ

UKSorry? or Pardon?
Cheers = thanks / goodbye
How do you do?
USExcuse me? or What was that?
Thanks
How are you doing?
Practice tip: each week watch a short video from a different English-speaking country and note two sounds that are different.

title: Advanced Conditionals
body_content:
Practice Advanced Conditionals.

Say it: inverted conditionals

Were it not for your help, we would have failed. Pause after the fronted clause and stress HELP. With Had I known the tone rises before the pause: Had I KNOWN ↗ | I would have CALLED.

Where accents differ

UKShould you need anything, please ring.
USShould you need anything, please call.
Say it: "Were it not for your help, we would have failed."

title: Subjunctive
body_content:
Practice Subjunctive.

Say it: the mandative subjunctive

After verbs like suggest, insist and recommend the bare form is used: I suggest that he BE early. The bare verb carries the stress. Also: If I WERE you.

Where accents differ

UKI suggest that he should be early. (with should)
USI suggest that he be early. (bare form preferred)
Say it: "I insist that she be told. I recommend that he leave early."

title: Cleft Sentences
body_content:
Practice Cleft Sentences.

Say it: focus stress in cleft sentences

In a cleft the focus takes the nuclear stress: It was JOHN who broke it. What I need is a HOLiday. The first part is quick and weak. The stress tells the listener what is new or corrected.

Where accents differ

UKWhat I need is a holiday.
USWhat I need is a vacation.
Say it: "It was John who broke it. What I need is a rest."

audio_urls.title: Say it: focus stress in cleft sentences

title: Inversion after Only
body_content:
Practice Inversion after Only.

Say it: the pause after Only

Keep only then as one chunk, stress THEN, pause briefly, then return to normal rhythm: Only THEN | did I realISE. The same works for Only after, Only when and Only by.

Where accents differ

UKrealise /ˈrɪəlaɪz/
USrealize /ˈriːəlaɪz/
Say it: "Only then did I realise. Only after the storm did we leave."

audio_urls.title: Say it: the pause after Only

title: Nominalisation
body_content:
Practice Nominalisation.

Say it: stress in nominalisation

Two-syllable words: verbs often take stress on the second syllable, nouns on the first: a REcord / to reCORD, an INcrease / to inCREASE. Suffixes move stress: deCIDE → deCIsion; imPROVE → imPROVEment.

Where accents differ

UKorganisation /ˌɔːɡənaɪˈzeɪʃn/
USorganization /ˌɔːrɡənəˈzeɪʃn/
Say it: "There was an increase. Prices increase. A record; to record."

title: Academic Stance
body_content:
Practice Academic Stance.

Listen for: stance and hedging in tone

Speakers signal stance with tone and hedges: It could be argued that..., The evidence suggests..., arguably. A fall-rise marks caution: This is ↘↗arguably the strongest case. Strong stance uses clear stress: It clearly DOES.

Listen for: "This is arguably the strongest case. The evidence suggests otherwise."

title: Academic Writing Integration

revision.summary: An integrative revision lesson combining nominalisation, academic stance, and discourse markers for learners consolidating academic writing skills.
examples: Turning verbs into nouns can make writing sound more formal and academic.
Discourse markers like 'however' and 'furthermore' help structure an argument.

body_content:
An integrative revision lesson combining nominalisation, academic stance, and discourse markers for learners consolidating academic writing skills.

Examples

  • Turning verbs into nouns can make writing sound more formal and academic.
  • Discourse markers like 'however' and 'furthermore' help structure an argument.

Key terms

  • nominalisation
  • academic stance
  • discourse markers

Say it: reading discourse markers aloud

Read your paragraph aloud: a signpost like however or furthermore gets a short pause and a small rise before the new idea. If it sounds awkward aloud, it may read awkwardly.

Where accents differ

UKwhilst, amongst
USwhile, among
Say it: "However, the data suggest otherwise. Furthermore, the sample was small."

audio_urls.title: Say it: reading discourse markers aloud

title: Past Perfect
body_content:
Practice Past Perfect.

Listen for: 'd had or 'd would

In fast speech had becomes 'd, easy to confuse with would: I'd finished vs I'd finish. Listen to what follows: a past participle means had, a base verb means would. She'd already gone /ʃiːd ɔːlˈredi ɡɒn/.

Where accents differ

UKI'd not seen him for years.
USI hadn't seen him in years.
Listen for: "I'd finished before she'd arrived. I'd finish it if I could."

title: Modal verbs
body_content:
Practice Modal verbs.

Say it: can and can't

The vowel and stress separate can from can't. Positive can is weak /kən/: I can COME. Negative can't is strong /kɑːnt/ (UK) and the verb is weak: I CAN'T come. In US speech the /t/ may vanish, so listen to the vowel and context.

Where accents differ

UKcan't /kɑːnt/
UScan't /kænt/
Say it: "I can come on Friday. I can't come on Saturday."

title: Ellipsis and elision
body_content:
Practice Ellipsis and elision.

Listen for: elision and ellipsis

Elision drops sounds: next day /neks deɪ/, friendship /ˈfrenʃɪp/. Ellipsis drops words: (Have you) got a minute? (I'm) sorry. Listen for the stressed words; the missing ones can be inferred.

Where accents differ

UKFancy a cuppa? (Do you fancy a...)
USWant some coffee? (Do you want...)
Listen for: "Got a minute? Sorry, can't stop."

title: Question tags
body_content:
Practice Question tags.

Say it: rising and falling tags

A falling tag asks for agreement: It's cold, isn't it ↘. A rising tag is a real question: You've got the keys, haven't you ↗? Keep the tag light: /ˈɪznt ɪt/. A positive-positive tag shows surprise or suspicion: So you're leaving, are you?

Where accents differ

UKYou're coming, aren't you?
USYou're coming, right?
Say it: "It's cold, isn't it? You've got the keys, haven't you?"

audio_urls.title: Say it: rising and falling tags

title: Relative clauses
body_content:
Practice Relative clauses.

Listen for: defining and non-defining pauses

Non-defining clauses are marked by pauses and a lower voice: My car, | which I bought last year, | keeps breaking down. Defining clauses flow: The car that I bought last year keeps breaking down. Listen for which speakers use a pause to add extra information.

Where accents differ

UKThe man whom I met (formal)
USThe man that I met (usual)
Listen for: "My sister, who lives in Rome, is a nurse. The sister who lives in Rome is a nurse."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: defining and non-defining pauses

title: Nostalgia
body_content:
Practice Nostalgia.

Listen for: tone in nostalgic speech

Nostalgic speech is slower, with longer pauses and a softer, falling tone: Those were the days. Listen for used to /ˈjuːst tə/ and would for habit: We'd spend hours by the RIVer. Signal words: back then, in those days, I remember.

Where accents differ

UKWe used to buy sweets after school.
USWe used to buy candy after school.
Listen for: "Back then, we'd spend hours by the river. Those were the days."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: tone in nostalgic speech

title: Age and cultural differences
body_content:
Practice Age and cultural differences.

Listen for: tone across cultures

Intonation can be read differently across cultures: a rise at the end of a statement may be politeness, uncertainty or a check, not always a question. Listen to the pattern and the context. Notice how direct requests sound (Could you...? vs Would you mind...?).

Listen for: "Would you mind waiting a moment? Could you send it today?"

title: Current affairs
body_content:
Practice Current affairs.

Listen for: the style of news reports

News reports are fast, with stress on names, numbers and verbs: The GOVernment has ANnounced a NEW tax. Listen for reporting verbs and hedges: allegedly, is expected to, sources say.

Where accents differ

UKMP, Prime Minister, the Commons
USCongress, the President, the White House
Listen for: "The government has announced a new tax, which is expected to rise next year."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: the style of news reports

title: Moral and personal dilemmas
body_content:
Practice Moral and personal dilemmas.

Say it: weighing options aloud

Dilemmas use balanced phrases with stress on the contrast: On the ONE hand... | on the OTHer... Raise your pitch on the first option and fall on the second. Hedges soften: I suppose, it depends, I'm torn.

Say it: "On the one hand, it's honest. On the other, it could hurt her."

revision.summary: Practice Road and home safety and risk.

title: Environmental issues
body_content:
Practice Environmental issues.

Say it: word stress in environmental vocabulary

Stress in long words: enVIronment, susTAINable, deforeSTAtion, bioDIVersity. Say the stressed syllable longer and louder and reduce the others.

Where accents differ

UKaluminium /ˌæljəˈmɪniəm/
rubbish, bin
USaluminum /əˈluːmɪnəm/
trash, garbage can
Say it: "Deforestation threatens biodiversity. We need sustainable energy."

audio_urls.title: Say it: word stress in environmental vocabulary

title: Architecture
body_content:
Practice Architecture.

Say it: stress in architecture words

Stress moves: ARchitect, archiTECture, archiTECtural. Façade /fəˈsɑːd/, Gothic /ˈɡɒθɪk/.

Where accents differ

UKbaroque /bəˈrɒk/
lift, ground floor
USbaroque /bəˈroʊk/
elevator, first floor
Say it: "The architect designed a Gothic façade. Architecture shapes a city."

audio_urls.title: Say it: stress in architecture words

title: Advising
body_content:
Practice Advising.

Say it: softening advice

Soften advice with modals and a gentle tone: You might want to..., If I were you, I'd..., Have you thought of...? A rise-fall sounds friendly; a flat fall can sound like an order.

Where accents differ

UKWhy don't you speak to her?
USYou may want to speak to her.
Say it: "If I were you, I'd speak to her. Have you thought of asking?"

revision.summary: Practice Expressing opinions formally and informally.

title: Expressing annoyance
body_content:
Practice Expressing annoyance.

Say it: annoyance and control

Annoyance shows in wider pitch and extra stress on the emphasised word: How MANy times do I have to TELL you? You're ALways leaving the door open! At C1, keep it controlled: a low, level tone can sound colder than a loud one.

Where accents differ

UKIt's driving me mad.
USIt's driving me crazy.
Say it: "How many times do I have to tell you? You're always late!"

revision.summary: Practice Describing people and things and situations.

title: Rhythm and Chunking

revision.summary: Control English stress-timed rhythm and split speech into meaningful chunks (thought groups) with a clear main stress, so you sound fluent and are easy to follow.
examples: I'd like to talk about | the results | of the survey.
Content words carry the beat; function words shrink.

body_content:
Rhythm and Chunking

Advanced speakers are often understood or misunderstood because of rhythm, not single sounds. English is stress-timed: stressed syllables come at fairly regular beats, and the syllables between them are squeezed together.

1. Beat and weak words

Content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) carry the beat. Function words (the, of, and, to, can) are weak. Compare: The RESULTS of the SURvey were SURprising. Four beats, even though the number of syllables changes.

2. Chunking

Fluent speech is delivered in chunks (thought groups) of about three to seven words, each with a short pause or a change of pitch at the end:

I'd like to talk about | the results | of the survey | we ran in March.

Pausing inside a chunk (for example between of and the survey) sounds hesitant and can confuse the listener.

3. Nuclear stress

Each chunk has one nuclear (main) stress, usually on the last content word: the reSULTS, we ran in MARCH. Move it to show contrast: I said the RESULTS, not the method.

4. Where accents differ

Word stress and vowel reduction change the rhythm of the same word:

UKlaboratory /ləˈbɒrətri/ (4 syllables)
secretary /ˈsekrətri/
schedule /ˈʃedjuːl/
USlaboratory /ˈlæbrətɔːri/ (5 syllables)
secretary /ˈsekrəteri/
schedule /ˈskedʒuːl/
Practice tip: mark a paragraph with | for chunk boundaries and underline the nuclear stress in each chunk. Read it aloud, tapping the beat.

title: Discourse Intonation

revision.summary: Use pitch to signal new versus shared information, contrast, reservations and topic changes, and read the attitude behind other speakers' intonation.
examples: fall-rise = shared information or a reservation ("Well, it's interesting...")
higher key = contrast or a new topic

body_content:
Discourse Intonation

At C1 intonation does more than mark statements and questions. Pitch shows how a speaker treats information and how they feel about it.

1. Falling tone: telling

A fall on the nuclear syllable presents new information: The meeting is on ↘FRIday. It sounds certain and complete.

2. Fall-rise: shared ground or a reservation

A fall-rise (↘↗) marks information the listener already knows, or a point the speaker is not fully committed to:

A: What did you think of the proposal?
B: Well, it's ↘↗interesting... (but I have doubts)

A flat, polite reply with a fall-rise on interesting often means I am not convinced.

3. Key: starting high or low

Starting a chunk higher than the previous one signals a new topic or contrast (Now, on a DIFFerent note...). A lower start signals an aside or something less important.

4. Where accents differ

The same patterns exist, but frequency and use vary:

UKThe fall-rise for polite reservations is very common (Well, it's ↘↗interesting)
Statements usually end with a fall
Sorry? with a rise to ask for repetition
USA rising end on statements (uptalk) is common in some varieties and does not always mean a question
Reservations are often stated more directly
Excuse me? / Pardon? to ask for repetition
Practice tip: listen to one speaker for two minutes. Note three falls, one fall-rise and one high start, and decide what each one signals.

title: Listening: Fast Speech

revision.summary: Practise following fast, informal speech with reductions, weak forms and blurred word boundaries, using context and stressed words rather than trying to catch every word.

body_content:
Listening: Fast Speech

Native speakers do not pronounce every word. In fast speech, function words shrink, words join together and some sounds disappear. Successful listeners rely on stressed words and context.

1. Script 1: making plans

A: D'you wanna grab a coffee after work?
B: I've gotta finish this report first, but I should be done by six.
A: Kinda late for coffee, though. Wanna get dinner instead?
B: Sure, I dunno anywhere good near here, though.

Decode: D'you wanna = Do you want to; gotta = (have) got to; kinda = kind of; dunno = I don't know.

2. Strategies

  • Listen for the stressed content words first: coffee, report, six, dinner.
  • Expect weak forms and contractions: could've, should've, whatcha.
  • If you miss a word, keep listening and use context. Do not stop to translate.
  • Listen again and compare what you heard with the full forms.

3. Script 2: a voicemail

Hey, it's me. Listen, I'm gonna be a bit late, so don't wait for me. I'll grab something on the way. See ya in a bit.

Main idea: the speaker will arrive late and will bring food or a snack.

4. Where UK and US differ

Reductions exist in both, but some forms are more typical of one:

UKinnit (isn't it), ta (thanks)
I've got to = I've gotta
The /t/ in a lot of is often clear
USwhaddaya (what do you), lemme (let me)
I gotta (without have)
The /t/ in a lot of often sounds like /d/: "a lodda"
Practice tip: play ten seconds of a casual conversation three times. First for the topic, then for the stressed words, then write what you heard and check it.

title: Listening: Academic Lectures

revision.summary: Follow the structure of an academic lecture using signposting language and stressed key terms, take effective notes, and recognise UK and US university vocabulary.
examples: Today I'll focus on three causes.
To sum up, the evidence suggests...

body_content:
Listening: Academic Lectures

Lectures are long and dense, but they are organised. The lecturer tells you the structure with signposting language and stresses the key terms. Your job is to catch the structure, not every word.

1. Script 1: opening a lecture

Good morning. Today I'll focus on three causes of urban migration: economic opportunity, education and family networks. I'll begin with the economic factors, and then, turning to education, I'll explain why cities attract younger people.

Notes: Urban migration: 3 causes = 1 economic, 2 education, 3 family.

2. Signposting language

  • Today I'll focus on / There are three main... = overview.
  • Turning to / Moving on to = a new point.
  • In contrast / However = a different or opposite idea.
  • For instance / Take, for example = an example.
  • To sum up / In conclusion = the end.

3. Script 2: a contrast

Early studies suggested that migration was driven by wages alone. In contrast, more recent research shows that family ties matter just as much. For instance, in one survey, more than half of migrants moved to join relatives.

Notes: Early: wages only. Recent: family ties too (survey: over 50% joined relatives).

4. Note-taking tips

Write key terms and numbers, use symbols (→ cause, ≠ different, ↑ increase) and leave space to add details later.

5. Where UK and US differ

UKlecture, seminar, tutor
module (a unit of a course)
timetable, revision
USclass, lecture, professor
course (a unit of study)
schedule, review
Practice tip: play a two-minute lecture extract. Write only the signposting words you hear, then use them to reconstruct the structure.

title: Nuanced Modality
body_content:
Practice Nuanced Modality.

Say it: stress and modal nuance

Stressing the modal signals doubt or contrast: He COULD do it (but will he?). Stressing the main verb states the action: He could DO it. Weak forms: could have /kʊd əv/, might have /maɪt əv/.

Where accents differ

UKshan't, needn't
USwon't, don't need to
Say it: "He could do it. He might have left. She must have known."

audio_urls.title: Say it: stress and modal nuance

title: Fronting
body_content:
Practice Fronting.

Say it: fronting and stress

Fronted words get the stress and often a slight pause: Never before have I SEEN it. Rich, she was not. Into the room walked a STRANGer. Read the fronted phrase, pause, then deliver the rest.

Say it: "Never before had she seen such a view. Into the room walked a stranger."

title: Semantic Nuance
body_content:
Practice Semantic Nuance.

Listen for: shades of meaning in stress

Stress shows the shade of meaning: I didn't say she STOLE it (someone else did); I didn't say she stole IT (something else). Listen for the stressed word to find the speaker's exact point.

Where accents differ

UKquite (moderately)
USquite (very)
Listen for: "I didn't say she stole it."

audio_urls.title: Listen for: shades of meaning in stress

title: Pragmatics
body_content:
Practice Pragmatics.

Listen for: implied meaning

Listen for what is not said. Well, it's ↘↗interesting may mean disagreement. I'll think about it can mean no. A pause before answering, a hedge (well, sort of) or a lowered voice signals an answer the speaker would rather avoid. Ask: what did the speaker avoid saying?

Where accents differ

UKQuite good (may be weak praise)
USPretty good
Listen for: "Well, it's interesting. I'll think about it."

title: Register and Tone
body_content:
Practice Register and Tone.

Say it: register in speech

Formal speech uses fuller forms and careful articulation: I am unable to attend. Informal speech uses contractions and reductions: I can't make it. Say a formal sentence, then re-say it informally, changing the words and the speed.

Where accents differ

UKDear Sir or Madam, Yours faithfully
USTo whom it may concern, Sincerely
Say it: "I am unable to attend. / I can't make it."

title: Intonation: Attitude and Nuance

revision.summary: Use pitch range, tone and stress to signal irony, politeness, doubt, enthusiasm and detachment, and to recognise the attitude behind what a speaker says.

body_content:
Intonation: Attitude and Nuance

At C2 the words are often the smaller part of the message. The same sentence can be warm, polite, ironic or dismissive depending on pitch range, tone and stress.

1. Wide or narrow pitch

A wide range (big jumps up and down) sounds engaged and enthusiastic: That's a ↗FANtastic idea! A narrow, flat range sounds bored, cold or sarcastic: Oh, great. Same words, opposite meaning.

2. Tone changes meaning

A: I've booked the 6 a.m. train.
B: Really? ↗ (surprised, interested)
B: Really. ↘ (flat: I am not pleased)

A fall-rise can soften disagreement or show reluctance: I suppose ↘↗so.

3. Stress and understatement

Stress can hint at what is not said: It was a ↘BIT expensive (= very expensive). Understatement plus a flat tone is a marker of irony, especially in British English.

4. Where accents differ

Norms of pitch and directness vary:

UKUnderstatement and a flat tone often mean the opposite: Not bad can be high praise
Quite good may be lukewarm
Polite disagreement: I'm not sure that's quite right
USA wider pitch range and stronger enthusiasm are common: That's great! may be simple politeness
Pretty good is usually positive
Disagreement is often more direct: I don't think so
Practice tip: choose one neutral sentence and say it four ways: enthusiastic, bored, sarcastic, doubtful. Record yourself and check that a listener could name each attitude.

title: Listening: Implication, Irony and Accents

revision.summary: Follow what speakers imply rather than say, recognise irony and understatement, and cope with a range of native and non-native accents using context and attitude cues.
examples: That went well. (after a disaster: irony)
I don't suppose you could... (an indirect request)
Not the brightest idea. (understatement = a bad idea)

body_content:
Listening: Implication, Irony and Accents

At the highest level you must hear what the speaker means, not only what they say. Listen for mismatches between the words, the tone and the situation.

1. Script 1: irony

A: How was the presentation?
B: Oh, it went brilliantly. The projector died, the slides were in the wrong order, and I forgot the client's name.

The words say brilliantly, but the facts show the opposite. The listener concludes: it went badly.

2. Script 2: implication and indirect requests

A: It's getting rather warm in here.
B: I'll open a window.

A does not ask, but implies a request. Other indirect forms: I don't suppose you could..., Would it be a problem if..., It would be great if...

3. Understatement

  • Not the brightest idea = a very bad idea.
  • A slight problem = a serious problem.
  • Not exactly cheap = expensive.

4. Listening to different accents

Do not expect the accent in your practice recordings. Listen for stressed words and repeated patterns, and adjust after the first few sentences. Familiar text is easier: read the transcript afterwards, then listen again.

5. Where UK and US differ

UKIrony is often dry and delivered with a straight face
Quite can weaken (quite good = fairly good)
brilliant, cheers, rubbish
USIrony is often marked by exaggerated tone
Quite is rare; pretty is used instead
awesome, thanks, garbage
Practice tip: listen to a two-minute interview and note one thing said directly and one thing only implied. Then check the transcript.
